blocks.text: Let several identical consumers pull from one queue, so throughput scales by adding consumers and each message goes to one of them.

Producers write to a single **queue**. A pool of interchangeable **consumers** each take the next message, process it, and acknowledge it. The broker hands every message to one consumer, so adding or removing consumers changes capacity without touching producers.

items: **Gives up:** ordering across consumers, unless you partition by key.

blocks.text: Delivery is almost always at-least-once: a consumer that crashes before acking causes redelivery. Consumers must tolerate duplicates.

walkthrough.note: A job is an immutable record. `STOP` is a sentinel (poison pill) compared by identity, so it can never collide with real work.
Each worker loops on `take()`. The queue is the only shared coordination point: whoever calls `take()` first owns that job. Workers share no other state about which job is whose.
One shared `LinkedBlockingQueue`, plus thread-safe bookkeeping used only to verify that no job was handled twice.
Four identical consumers start on virtual threads. Scaling out is changing `workers`; nothing else knows the number.
The producer only enqueues. It does not know how many consumers exist or which one will take a job.
One `STOP` per consumer lets each exit its loop. Leaving the `try` block waits for all workers, so the printout is deterministic.

blocks.text: A photo app publishes one `PhotoUploaded` message per upload to a queue. Traffic is spiky: ten times the load on Sunday evenings. A single worker falls hours behind, so the team runs the same worker image as N replicas on the same queue and scales N from queue depth. A message that fails three times moves to a dead-letter queue.

lines: // every replica runs the same loop against queue "thumbnails"

blocks.text: Payoff: Sunday peaks are absorbed by adding replicas, and a crashed worker just means its message reappears for another one.

lists.title: Use when
items: Jobs are independent and one worker cannot keep up.
Load is spiky and you want to scale workers on queue depth.
A slow or crashed worker must not stall the others.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Messages must be processed in strict global order.
Every message must reach every subscriber: that is publish/subscribe.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Acking before processing loses work on a crash; acking after causes duplicates.
A poison message retried forever blocks capacity: set a retry limit and a dead-letter queue.
Ordering needs partitioning by key, which caps parallelism at the partition count.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Adding consumers when the bottleneck is the database they all write to.
Competing consumers on a queue that carries only a handful of messages per hour.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Virtual threads make one thread per in-flight message cheap, so a blocking consumer loop is fine.
`ExecutorService` with `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` gives structured start and shutdown, as in the sample.

rows.difference: Producer-Consumer is the in-process hand-off through a bounded buffer. Competing Consumers applies it across processes with a broker, acknowledgements, redelivery and scale-out.
A thread pool shares a work queue among threads of one JVM and loses the queue on exit. Competing consumers share a durable queue among separate processes.
Observer or pub/sub delivers each event to every subscriber. Competing consumers deliver each message to exactly one member of the group.
At-least-once delivery means a message can reach a second consumer after a timeout. Each consumer must be idempotent to make that harmless.
Separate queues and consumer pools per workload keep one slow job type from consuming all capacity.

entries.name: Work queues
entries.detail: Several consumers on one queue receive messages round-robin; `basic.ack` confirms and unacked messages are redelivered.

entries.name: Visibility timeout
entries.detail: A received message is hidden from other consumers until it is deleted or the timeout expires, then reappears.

entries.name: ThreadPoolExecutor
entries.detail: Worker threads compete for tasks from one `BlockingQueue`: the same idea inside a single JVM.

entries.name: Job with parallelism

exercises.prompt: Which pattern most directly fixes the backlog?

options.why: Independent jobs on one queue can be drained in parallel by adding identical workers, with no producer change.
Limiting intake lowers the arrival rate but does not drain the backlog; capacity must grow.
Isolating pools protects other workloads but adds no throughput for this one.
A gateway sits in front of synchronous client calls and does nothing for background job throughput.

modelAnswer.text: Several identical workers read one queue and each message goes to one of them, so you scale by adding workers. Delivery is at-least-once: unacknowledged messages are redelivered, so handlers must be idempotent and ordering is lost. Pub/sub instead copies each message to every subscriber.

keyPoints: Many identical consumers on one queue; each message goes to one
Scale out by adding consumers, producers unaffected
At-least-once delivery means redelivery and duplicates
Handlers should be idempotent; ordering is not guaranteed
Pub/sub fans out to all subscribers instead
